title: Repo-digest LLM regeneration has no rate limit, cooldown, or budget accounting
detail: RepoDigestCache.current() (packages/server/src/orchestrator/repoDigest.ts:158-168) is called synchronously from Orchestrator.orientationFor() on every dispatch() and resumeRun() call. Whenever the checkout's HEAD has moved since the cached digest was written, it fires a background LLM generation (generateRepoDigest — a full read-only Agent SDK turn that reads repo files, not a cheap completion). The only throttle is a single-flight `refreshing` boolean that prevents two generations from overlapping; there is no minimum interval between successive generations, no cap on how often HEAD is allowed to trigger a regeneration, and no config toggle to disable the feature (grepped packages/core/src/config.ts and .dispatch/config.yml — nothing references digest). Unlike every other LLM-driven path in this codebase, this call is never checked against orchestrator.maxBudgetUsd (that cap is only threaded into startAndRegister's executor options in dispatch()/resumeRun()/dispatchAuxRun()). In the exact scenario this codebase is built around — an EpicEngine auto-dispatching many tasks whose runs squash-merge into the main checkout via the merge queue, each merge advancing HEAD — every merge can trigger another full-repo-read LLM call with no operator control over frequency or cost.

title: Digest generation failures are silent — no ledger/UI surfacing, unlike the established degradation pattern
detail: RepoDigestCache.refresh()'s catch handler (packages/server/src/orchestrator/repoDigest.ts:187-191) only does `console.error` on a generation failure (missing CLI, model error, etc.), and retries silently on the next dispatch — forever, if the underlying cause doesn't clear. This codebase already has an established convention for exactly this situation: DepMapCache's `onDegrade` callback (wired in packages/server/src/index.ts around the depMapCache construction) writes a `kind: 'hazard'` LedgerStore entry when carto degrades, so the failure is visible to a human via the app, not just server logs. The new digest cache has no equivalent — an operator whose digest generation is persistently broken (e.g. bad API key, no CLI on PATH in the daemon's environment) has no way to discover why the '## Repo orientation' section never gets a repo map, short of reading dispatchd's stdout.

title: Non-empty concurrent-runs prompt text drops the 'check again later' caveat the empty case has
detail: orientation.ts's renderConcurrentRuns (packages/server/src/orchestrator/orientation.ts:304-324) explicitly tells the agent, when nobody else is running, to 'call run_list only if you need a fresher answer later in your work.' When runs ARE listed, that caveat disappears — prompt.ts's orientation-present branch (packages/server/src/orchestrator/prompt.ts:101-105) instead states flatly 'Concurrency is already reported above, so you do not need to open with `run_list`,' with no reminder that this is a point-in-time snapshot taken before the agent's very first turn (dispatch() collects concurrentRuns synchronously before startAndRegister). For a long-running task, this asymmetry nudges the agent to treat stale-by-design concurrency data as settled fact for the whole run, which is exactly the collision risk run_list exists to catch (a new run getting dispatched on an overlapping file mid-task).

title: Stop escalation is a flat wall-clock timer, not tied to whether the agent actually kept working
detail: The confirmed design (per the task's Activity log) is: "a stop auto-escalates to a hard cancel if the agent keeps calling tools past a timeout." scheduleStopEscalation (orchestrator.ts:1045) does not implement that condition — it arms a single setTimeout(STOP_ESCALATION_MS = 120_000) at the moment requestStop() is called, and unconditionally falls back to cancel() if the run is still non-terminal 2 minutes later, with no check on whether the agent has issued any NEW tool call since the stop (which canUseTool would have denied) versus still being legitimately mid-way through the ONE tool call that was already in flight when Stop was pressed — the exact call graceful stop explicitly promises not to abort (see the STOP_ESCALATION_MS doc comment: "the agent may legitimately be mid-tool-call (a long test run, a large edit) when Stop is pressed, and that call is exactly what a graceful stop promises not to abort"). If that one legitimate in-flight operation (a long test suite, a large refactor, a slow build) takes longer than 2 minutes, the escalation timer fires anyway and calls cancel(), which — unlike the graceful finish path — skips handleFinish's auto-commit and leaves whatever that operation produced uncommitted and discarded. This silently converts a well-behaved graceful stop into the same data-losing outcome as a hard Cancel, for the exact scenario the feature was designed to protect. Confirmed by reading scheduleStopEscalation's implementation directly; the only test covering this path (stop.test.ts's 'does not cancel a run that wound down before the window elapsed') exercises a stop that finishes quickly, not a single in-flight operation that legitimately outlives the window, so this gap has no test coverage either.

title: "Stopped" chip doesn't distinguish a clean graceful stop from an escalated hard cancel
detail: deriveStopControl (apps/desktop/src/lib/runState.ts:150) sets showStoppedChip purely from `!live && stopRequestedAt !== undefined`, with no check on which terminal state the run actually landed in. Because stopRequestedAt is set once and never cleared (per its own doc comment: "never cleared — a stop cannot be taken back, only escalated to a hard cancel"), a run that gets escalated to cancel() by scheduleStopEscalation (see the related finding) ends up with state 'cancelled' AND stopRequestedAt set, so RunDetailHeader renders the same 'Stopped' chip (tooltip: 'Stop requested at <time>') as a run that wound down cleanly and had its work auto-committed. The two outcomes are materially different for the user — one preserves the agent's work as reviewable, the other discards it exactly like pressing Cancel — but the header gives no visual signal of which one happened; only digging into the Activity log (which does log 'escalating to cancel') reveals the difference. Confirmed by reading deriveStopControl and RunDetailHeader.tsx directly; runState.test.ts's coverage for a terminal+stopRequestedAt run only exercises the 'finished' case, not 'cancelled'.

title: Warden action confirm is authorized at 'request' tier, so the agent token can approve the warden's queued mutating actions
detail: POST /api/warden/:id/actions/:actionId/confirm is an adjudication route — WardenMessage's own docs say a queued action settles 'once a human decides', and index.ts's new wiring comment calls the registry 'the confirmation gate'. But the route was not added to DECIDE_TIER_ROUTES (packages/server/src/api.ts:3467), whose comment explicitly says 'a new decision-class route is an entry here'. requiredTier() therefore returns 'request' for it, which the agentToken satisfies — the token written to the 0600 daemon file that every dispatched agent, the CLI, and MCP read. Verified empirically: I booted a real server from this checkout in a scratch temp repo, queued a dispatch_task action via a FakeWarden, and confirmed it with `Authorization: Bearer <agentToken>` — the request returned 200 and the run was dispatched, while the analogous POST /api/runs/:id/scope-requests/:id/decide with the same token correctly returned 403. Consequence: any agent-token holder can approve (or deny) warden actions, and the record then tells the model and the transcript 'the human approved this' (warden.ts's settleAction), corrupting the human-decision audit trail the feature is built around. Rated important rather than critical only because the agent token can already reach the underlying mutations (dispatch, merge-queue ops) directly through other request-tier routes, so there is no net privilege escalation — the hole is in the confirmation gate's integrity, not in raw capability. The fix is one entry in DECIDE_TIER_ROUTES; the desktop app holds the appToken ('decide') so nothing user-facing changes.

title: Confirm does not 409 while a turn is running, deviating from the acceptance criterion's 'same busy error shapes' as plan/draft confirm
detail: The task says the confirm endpoint should behave 'like sendDraftMessage/confirm, with the same busy/not-found error shapes as the existing plan/draft endpoints'. PlanManager.confirm throws OrchestratorConflictError (409) when the plan is 'running' (packages/server/src/orchestrator/plan.ts:394), but WardenManager.confirmAction deliberately allows confirming while a turn is in flight (packages/server/src/orchestrator/warden.ts:300, pre-existing code this diff exposes). The rationale documented there — a human should not have to wait for the assistant to finish talking before approving a cancel — is sound, and the record-bookkeeping helpers re-read state so a mid-turn confirm does not corrupt the transcript. But it is a deviation from the stated criterion, no test pins the confirm-while-running behavior either way, and the human should rule on which contract is intended. Not-found shapes do match (404 via the shared OrchestratorNotFoundError mapping, verified by test and by run).

title: Client ServerEvent union claims to mirror events.ts 'exactly' but has no 'warden.changed' member
detail: packages/client/src/api.ts's ServerEvent union (line 543) declares in multiple comments that it 'mirrors packages/server/src/events.ts exactly', but it contains no 'warden.changed' entry (grep for 'warden' in the file returns nothing), while the server union has carried it since the WardenManager task. This drift predates this diff — the diff did not touch events.ts — but this task's stated purpose is 'broadcast a warden.changed event ... so the desktop app can invalidate its query', and the desktop app cannot type or dispatch on an event its own ServerEvent union does not know. The server-side broadcast criterion is genuinely met (verified over a live websocket by the new test and confirmed in WardenManager.updateRecord/sendMessage), so this is a follow-up-wiring gap plus a now-false 'mirrors exactly' comment, not a broken server behavior.

title: Orphan work committed while the daemon was down is never flagged — the cutoff is the boot force-fail, not the moment the daemon lost the run
detail: surveyRun's post-fail cutoff is firstFailedAt(), the ts of the FIRST 'failed' state line in the transcript (orchestrator.ts:1328/1364). For a boot force-fail that line is written by reconcileOnBoot with `const now = new Date().toISOString()` at BOOT time (orchestrator.ts:2549-2552), not at the time dispatchd died. The filter is `Date.parse(c.date) > failedAtMs`, so every commit the orphaned agent authored during the outage sorts before the cutoff and is discarded. Concretely: dispatchd dies at 12:00 while an agent is running, the orphan finishes and commits at 12:20, the user reopens the app at 13:00 — the run is force-failed at 13:00 with an empty postFailCommits, and the UI shows exactly the '$0 dead run' the task exists to eliminate, with the work sitting unannounced on the branch. Only the narrow window where the daemon comes back BEFORE the orphan commits (the r-96f433 case study, restart 4 min in, commit at 19:40) is covered. A cutoff derived from the run's last recorded activity (last transcript entry ts) rather than the boot stamp would cover both. I established this by reading reconcileOnBoot, firstFailedAt and the filter, and confirming the new tests only exercise the commit-after-boot ordering (survey.test.ts pins the commit's author date 60s into the FUTURE precisely to stay on the right side of this cutoff).

title: A force-failed run upgraded to interrupted-dirty is permanently excluded from orphan-work detection
detail: Both re-survey gates require state === 'failed' exactly: scheduleOrphanRecheck returns early unless `meta.state === 'failed'` (orchestrator.ts:1431) and surveyAndUpgradeIfDirty returns early on `meta.state !== 'failed'` (orchestrator.ts:1484), which even a forced resurveyOrphanWork() cannot bypass. But an agent that is alive at daemon restart is usually mid-edit, so the boot survey finds a dirty tree and upgrades the run to 'interrupted-dirty'. From that point nothing ever re-surveys it: when the orphan finishes and commits, no postFailCommits are computed, no banner appears, no activity note is written, and the stamped survey keeps listing uncommitted paths that no longer exist. This is arguably the more common shape of the very scenario the task describes (the agent was actively working when dispatchd restarted) and it gets zero coverage. No test covers an interrupted-dirty run gaining commits.

title: postFailCommits is computed over the worktree's whole HEAD history, not the run's own commits, so a restack turns base-branch commits into fake 'orphan work'
detail: surveyRun calls `repo.log({ limit: 50 })` with no ref and no range (orchestrator.ts:1342), which is `git log HEAD` in the run's worktree — it includes every ancestor, base branch included, not just `baseBranch..HEAD`. The only filter is the author date. That is safe while the branch never moves, but MergeQueue restacks failed runs: isRestackCandidate (mergeQueue.ts:1300) only requires `reviewedAt === undefined && baseDiscarded !== true && !worktreeIsBusy`, all true of a force-failed run, and restackStaleRun is seeded for every run at boot (mergeQueue.ts:294). A stacked run that was force-failed and whose blocker later merges is rebased onto the blocker's base (restackRun -> repointRunBase -> worktrees.rebaseOnto), pulling in every commit main gained since — all authored after the fail. The next getRun then reports them as work the orphan landed: a green 'Work landed on this branch after the failure — 7 commits, latest: "chore(board): sync 1 task"' banner in the run log and review views, an inbox notice, and a permanent, wrong line in the task's Activity log (stampOrphanWork's note is not reversible). Scoping the log to the run's own commits (`baseBranch..HEAD`, or `--not <baseBranch>`) would remove the whole class.

title: Detection only fires when a human opens the run — no background sweep, so the silent-orphan case still depends on someone looking
detail: scheduleOrphanRecheck is called from exactly one place, getRun (orchestrator.ts:408), which in practice means a human opening the run detail (or an agent posting a task comment via commentAuthorFor). There is no timer or boot-repeat sweep. The boot survey itself is a one-shot snapshot taken seconds after restart, before an orphan has usually committed. So the case study's actual failure mode — nobody looked at the run for six days while the board said in-progress — still produces no inbox notice and no activity note until somebody opens the run that already looks dead. This meets AC2 literally (the run detail is distinguishable once opened) but not the discovery half of the task's intent.

title: Stamping orphan work rewrites updatedAt, moving an old failed run's timestamp (and its cost) into the present
detail: stampOrphanWork does `registry.updateMeta(meta.id, { survey, updatedAt: now })` and appends a state line stamped `now` (orchestrator.ts:1532-1538), so replay carries it too. updatedAt is user-visible ordering and time data: ReviewQueue sorts on it (apps/desktop/src/components/runs/ReviewQueue.ts:81), AllAgentsView/TaskView sort and render 'x ago' from it, and App.tsx:380 sums costUsd into the current spend window via `new Date(r.updatedAt) >= start`. A run that failed weeks ago and then gets stamped reads as just-updated, jumps to the top of those lists, and folds its recorded cost into today's spend total. The survey/commit facts genuinely changed, so some marker is right — but reusing updatedAt overloads a field several unrelated surfaces trust as 'when this run last did something'.

title: getRun — a read path — can now flip a run's terminal state and post an activity note as a side effect
detail: scheduleOrphanRecheck (orchestrator.ts:408) routes through the existing scheduleSurvey -> surveyAndUpgradeIfDirty, which does far more than compute postFailCommits: on a dirty tree it transitions the run to 'interrupted-dirty', writes a transcript state line, broadcasts run.changed/run.survey and appends '[run x] flagged interrupted-dirty: N uncommitted path(s) found' to the task. Before this change that upgrade only ran at boot or straight after handleFinish; now merely opening a failed run in the UI can trigger it, based on whatever is in that worktree at view time (a human poking around in it after the fact, leftover build output). A GET that mutates run state and writes to the task file is a surprising seam, and nothing in the new tests covers 'open a failed run whose worktree got dirty later'.

title: Neither new UI banner has a component test, though both components already have test suites
detail: RunLogView.tsx:236-257 (failure-reason banner + orphan banner) and RunReviewView.tsx:243-248 are the surfaces AC1 and AC2 are actually judged on, and both are untested: apps/desktop/src/components/runs/RunLogView.test.tsx and RunReviewView.test.tsx exist and were not touched (grep for 'postFail|survey' in them returns nothing; I ran all three desktop suites — 48 pass — and none exercise the new markup). The only coverage is postFailWorkLabel/runSurveyNotice in runState.test.ts, i.e. the string, not the rendering or the `state === 'failed' || state === 'interrupted-dirty'` gate on the error banner. Deleting either JSX block would leave every test green.

title: A failed warden record fetch renders a permanent phantom "warden working" row in the rail
detail: `wardenLive` in LiveRail.tsx:104-106 is `conversationId !== null && (record === undefined || record.state === 'running')`. `record === undefined` is not only "still loading right after start" as the comment claims — useWardenSession's query is `retry: false` (useWardenSession.ts:81), so any failed GET /api/warden/:id leaves `record` undefined and `recordError` set indefinitely. Warden conversations are held in an in-memory Map server-side (packages/server/src/orchestrator/warden.ts:138), so a dispatchd restart 404s the id the client still holds. In that state the Runs tab shows a pulsing StateDot with the title 'Warden' (no prompt, no timestamp — the `record !== undefined` guard on line 225 hides the time) claiming an agent is at work forever, and WardenChat's identical `busy` expression keeps the composer permanently disabled. `warden.recordError` is available on the session and is not consulted. The same expression is duplicated in two files (LiveRail.tsx:104 and WardenChat.tsx `busy`), so any fix has to be applied twice unless it is lifted into a shared helper.

title: A warden action queued for approval produces no signal anywhere on the rail's default tab
detail: A turn that queues a mutating action settles to `state: 'ready'` with a non-empty `pendingActions` (documented on WardenState in packages/client/src/api.ts:834-837). At that point `wardenLive` is false, so the Runs-tab warden row disappears, and the attention strip's count comes only from `buildInbox(runs, repoPrs, openQuestions)` (apps/desktop/src/lib/liveRail.ts:50-56) which knows nothing about the warden — I grepped `pendingActions` across apps/desktop/src and the only consumer is wardenThread.ts, i.e. the transcript itself. So with the rail on its default Runs tab, an approval the warden is blocked on is invisible: no row, no count, no badge. The task's framing is that the strip is "the rail's one always-on signal" and that approvals are the point of putting the warden in the rail; a queued approval a user never sees is the one state that most needs the signal. Rated important rather than minor because it is the feature's central path silently going dark, not a cosmetic gap.

title: The warden Runs row labels an in-flight turn with the conversation's opening prompt and creation time
detail: LiveRail.tsx:222 and :227 render `warden.record.prompt` and `formatRelativeTimeFromIso(warden.record.createdAt)` — both are conversation-level, not turn-level. Every other row in the list uses per-run values (`run.taskTitle`, `run.createdAt`), so the warden row reads the same way while meaning something different: after several follow-ups the row still shows the first question, and a turn that started ten seconds ago in an hour-old conversation renders as a pulsing 'working' dot next to '1h ago'. `record.updatedAt`, or the `at` of the last user message, is the value that matches what the row is claiming.

title: The collapsed strip's running-agent count excludes the live warden
detail: The collapsed branch (LiveRail.tsx:135-144) still counts only `live.length`. Its own comment calls this "the one thing the strip cannot drop: that agents are running at all", and the task's rationale for the Runs row is that "the warden is an agent". With the rail collapsed, a warden turn in flight is the one agent that vanishes entirely — no dot, no contribution to the count — which is exactly the disappearing-signal behaviour the collapsed strip was designed to prevent.

title: Switching rail tabs silently discards a typed warden message
detail: The rail mounts WardenChat only while `tab === 'warden'` (LiveRail.tsx:260), and the composer text lives in WardenChat's own `prompt`/`followUp` state (WardenChat.tsx). One click on 'Runs' unmounts it and the half-written question — plus any `startError`/`sendError` banner explaining why the last send failed — is gone with no warning; clicking back shows an empty box. The tab buttons sit two rows above the composer in a 15rem column, so this is an easy accidental click. The same class of loss was introduced on the full page too: WardenView previously kept those hooks above its daemon gate, so a transient `portError` left the draft intact when the gate flipped; now WardenChat is mounted below the gate (WardenView.tsx) and unmounts with it. Hoisting the draft state to App (beside the session) or keeping WardenChat mounted and hidden fixes both.

title: The rail's Warden tab has no daemon gate, so it answers with a raw internal error
detail: WardenView gates the whole chat behind `data.portLoading || data.portError || data.client === null` and renders `DaemonUnavailable` with a retry button. The rail renders WardenChat unconditionally and has no access to `data`, so while dispatchd is booting or down the Warden tab presents a live-looking composer; pressing Ask surfaces useWardenSession's internal string 'dispatchd client not ready' (useWardenSession.ts:86) in a red banner, with no retry affordance. It is caught rather than swallowed, so this is a degraded path rather than a broken one — but it is the one surface of the two that a user reaches by accident on app start.

title: The rail approve test never flushes the decision, leaving the post-approval UI unverified and an act() warning in the suite
detail: 'a pending warden action renders the confirm card in the rail and decides through the session' (LiveRail.test.tsx) clicks Approve and asserts synchronously on `decisions`, but never awaits the `confirmAction` promise. Running the file (`bun test src/components/shell/LiveRail.test.tsx`: 13 pass) prints 'An update to WardenChat inside a test was not wrapped in act(...)' — the `setDecidingId(null)` after resolution lands outside act. Consequences: nothing verifies what the card does after a decision (deciding spinner, Retry label, the `decideError` banner on a rejected confirm), and an un-awaited state update escaping into the next test is a known source of cross-test flake in this shared happy-dom global. Awaiting the click via `act`/`findBy*` closes both.

I reviewed the undeclared surface: the extraction is behaviour-preserving except for the state-lifetime change reported separately.

title: Built on a superseded base: main deleted LandingView and the Inbox's embedded merge queue, so this fix cannot land as written
detail: The branch's only unique commit is be0c7178 on top of merge-base cc903b9a. Since then main replaced the whole landing surface: `git ls-tree main apps/desktop/src/views` has LandingTableView.tsx + lib/landingView.ts and has NO LandingView.tsx or LandedView.tsx, and main's InboxView doc comment states the removal was deliberate — "Deliberately only the two lists: what is landing, and what already landed, is the Landing table's job — one destination for it rather than a second, partial copy of the queue under this one." main's InboxView contains no LandingView import and no mergeQueue reference at all. I reproduced the merge in a throwaway clone under /tmp (never against this checkout): `git merge main` yields CONFLICT (modify/delete) on apps/desktop/src/views/LandingView.tsx and LandingView.test.tsx (deleted on main, modified here) plus a content conflict in InboxView.test.tsx. Consequences: (a) requirements 1-3 (Landed/Failed split, legible error + Retry, one-line empty queue) are implemented in a component main no longer renders, so they never reach the shipped UI; (b) resolving the conflict by keeping this side resurrects the embedded queue composition main removed on purpose (the diff package's 7913 deletions are main's landing work, not this branch's); (c) requirement 4's stated rationale ("so the two sections tell one story") is void on main, where the queue section is not under the Inbox. Nothing in the implementer's report or the task activity flags that the base was stale.

title: "Failed to land" rows render the entire 4000-character failure reason inline, unclamped and with newlines collapsed
detail:
LandingView.tsx:334 renders `{h.reason ?? 'failed'}` in a plain

with only `break-words` — no line-clamp, no expander, and no `whitespace-pre-wrap`. The server caps `reason` at REASON_LIMIT = 4000 characters (packages/server/src/orchestrator/mergeQueue.ts:43, applied at :920 via truncateReason over `commandErrorText`, i.e. the stderr tail of the failing verify command), and history holds up to 20 terminal entries. A real failed `bun run test`/`oxlint` attempt therefore renders as a ~4000-character block, and because the reason's newlines are collapsed by HTML the multi-line command output becomes one run-on paragraph — several of these push the rest of the Inbox off-screen. The task asked for the error "full text on the row or expandable"; full text with no clamp and no whitespace handling satisfies the letter while re-creating the legibility problem the task exists to fix. The prior code truncated the reason into a 220px cell, so this is a change in behaviour, not a pre-existing state.

title: The badge's "suppressed while re-queued" guard is untested and lives outside the tested lib
detail: InboxView.tsx:160-165 computes the badge as `verifyFailed.has(run.id) && !queued.has(run.id)`, with `queued` derived inline from `project.mergeQueue?.entries` at :93. The task said pure derivation belongs in the small tested lib; `latestAttemptFailedRunIds` takes only history, so this second half of the rule sits in the view untested. I verified it is untested by mutation in a throwaway clone: deleting `!queued.has(item.run.id)` leaves all 3 InboxView tests passing (3 pass / 0 fail). The implementer's report claims the badge is "suppressed while re-queued" — that claim rests on no test, and the equivalent rule on the LandingView side (`queuedRunIds`) is the one that does have a lib test. A control mutation (forcing the badge on for every row) does fail the suite, so the badge's positive/negative assertions are not vacuous — only the suppression branch is unguarded.

title: "verify failed" badge is applied to every queue failure, and contradicts the stale grouping for PR-backed runs
detail: The badge text asserts a verify failure, but `latestAttemptFailedRunIds` flags any history entry with state 'failed'. The queue fails entries for reasons that are not verify at all: 'run no longer exists' (mergeQueue.ts:882), 'run was already reviewed outside the merge queue' (:887), 'the run this one was stacked on was discarded' (:896), plus rebase and merge errors (:920). Worse for requirement 4's "one story" goal: buildReviewQueue (apps/desktop/src/components/runs/ReviewQueue.ts:56) keeps any run with a `prUrl` in Needs review even after `reviewedAt` is set (the needsHumanLook check is skipped for PR-backed runs). So for a PR-dispatched run whose PR the poller marks merged while it sits in the queue, the queue files a 'run was already reviewed outside the merge queue' failure: LandingView classifies it as stale and hides it behind the disclosure, while InboxView badges the same run 'verify failed' in Needs review — the two sections disagree, which is exactly the state requirement 4 was added to remove.

title: The Retry error path is implemented but never tested
detail: retryFailed (LandingView.tsx:114-127) catches the thrown Error from `handleEnqueueMerge` and renders it as "Retry failed: <message>" on the row (:337-342). That is the whole point of the inline error handling — the server 409s on already-queued/already-reviewed/blocked-findings runs (mergeQueue.ts:544-556 via whyNotEnqueueable, thrown as OrchestratorConflictError) — yet LandingView.test.tsx only exercises the success path ('a failed row retries by re-enqueuing its run'). No test rejects the stub handler, so a regression that swallowed the error (or dropped the runId keying so the message showed on the wrong row) would go unnoticed. The task's own emphasis on a per-row Retry with the error legible makes this the branch most worth pinning.

title: InboxView badge test's comment claims a case the test does not exercise
detail: The comment above the new test (InboxView.test.tsx:124-126) says "A run whose failure was followed by a merged attempt gets no badge — latest attempt wins." The fixture's second run ('fine' / 'Never queued') has no history entry at all, so what is actually asserted is that a run with no queue history is unbadged — a much weaker claim that would still pass if the latest-attempt-wins logic were replaced by "any failure ever". The latest-attempt rule is covered in queueHistory.test.ts, so this is a documentation/coverage mismatch rather than a hole in the derivation, but the comment reads as evidence for a guard the test does not hold.
